title: An orderly account (Luke 1:1–4)
hookLine: Luke writes to Theophilus, lover of God, so he may know the certainty

cards: Most books of the Bible never tell you who wrote them, or why. They just begin. Luke is different.
Before a single angel appears, there's a preface: four verses that are one long, polished sentence in Greek, the kind that opened histories and medical treatises in that world.
The writer steps out from behind the curtain and tells you what he's doing. And he isn't writing to the world in general. He's writing to one person, by name.

teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a narration of the things that have been accomplished among us." The first thing he says: others have already tried this.
Then where his material came from: those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning, and ministers of the word. Luke doesn't claim to be an eyewitness himself.
He's a careful second-generation writer who has, in his words, diligently traced everything from the start.
And then: it seemed good to me also "to write to thee in order, most excellent Theophilus, That thou mayest know the verity of those words in which thou hast been instructed."
Theophilus is a Greek name: theos, God, and philos, friend or lover. Friend of God. Was he real?
Most excellent was a polite title for an official or a person of rank, so he may have been a patron who paid for the copying.

But since early centuries readers have noticed that anyone who loves God fits the name, and Saint Ambrose said as much. Both can be true. Theophilus already knows the story; Luke writes so he can stand on solid ground.
The Greek for verity is asphaleia: firmness, footing that won't slip.

teach.h: THAT THOU MAYEST KNOW THE VERITY.
teach.b: Luke's second volume, the Acts of the Apostles, is addressed to Theophilus too.

The Gospel never names its author; early Christian writers name Luke, the companion called the most dear physician in the Letter to the Colossians. For the next fifty days, we read his account in order.

how: Catholics hear the Gospel of Luke read through at Sunday Mass every third year (Year C), and Luke's preface is proclaimed on a Sunday in Ordinary Time; his feast day is October 18.

o: friend of God, the man Luke wrote his Gospel for
a Roman governor who put Paul on trial
a Greek doctor who taught Luke medicine

s: Luke says he was an eyewitness of everything he writes
he says he drew on eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, and traced it all carefully.
Luke addresses Acts to Theophilus too
Acts opens by addressing Theophilus again; the two books are a pair.
the Gospel names Luke as its author in its text
the text never names him; early Christian writers attribute it to Luke, Paul's companion.

games.q: you're Luke. many others have already written accounts of Jesus. what do you do?
o: trace everything carefully from the beginning and write an orderly account for Theophilus.
write a new story with no sources.
games.why: it seemed good to me also, he says, having traced all things from the beginning, to write to thee in order.

practice: Find one thing you're certain of. Not everything, just one thing you could stand on if the floor shook: that someone loves you, that a kindness was real, that God was there in a moment, that truth matters.
Let it come, and test it gently: does it hold? If you pray, thank God for that solid ground.

wordCard.voice: Theophilus. Friend of God, the man Luke addressed his careful, orderly account to, drawing on eyewitnesses from the beginning. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: Theophilus, friend of God or dear to God, from theos and philos.

carryVoice: Your line: written for you. Anyone who loves God fits the name Theophilus. Day four hundred forty-two.
